title: LG Energy Solution launches battery production in Lansing - electrive.com
content:
LG Energy Solution (LGES) has launched production at its new battery plant in Lansing, Michigan, USA. Originally a joint venture with GM, the factory now belongs entirely to the Korean cell manufacturer. LGES is expanding the site's focus: In addition to LFP cells for Tesla's stationary storage systems, NMC cells for Toyota EVs will also be produced there in the future.
Image: LG Energy Solution
The 91.5-hectare facility is expected to achieve an annual production capacity of over 35 GWh at full capacity. According to LGES, the company has invested more than two billion dollars in the site since 2022. Currently, the plant employs around 900 people, with plans to increase this number to up to 1,700 in the future.
The production launch is particularly significant given the plant’s history: Lansing was originally meant to be the third cell factory for
Ultium Cells
, the joint battery venture between
General Motors
and LGES.
However, towards the end of 2024, GM announced
that it would sell its stake in the nearly completed site to LGES.
This move did not, however, mark a complete withdrawal by GM from Ultium Cells. The joint ventures in Ohio and Tennessee remained unaffected by the transaction. GM cited the need to adapt its battery production capacities in a capital-efficient manner to the development of the EV market as one of the reasons for the decision.
The acquisition was finalised in May 2025 – at which point construction work was already 98 per cent complete, according to LGES. Since then, Lansing has been fully owned by the Korean battery cell manufacturer.
Toyota secures capacity from GM
Following GM’s exit from the project, LGES repurposed the site. In early 2025, it was announced that Toyota would transfer an existing battery order with LG Energy Solution to the Lansing plant. This gave the facility, previously tailored to GM, a new key customer from the automotive industry.
In the future, LGES will manufacture NMC cells containing nickel, manganese, and cobalt for Toyota at the Lansing plant. One of the intended vehicles is the all-electric
Toyota Highlander for the 2027 model year
. The three-row eSUV is set to be produced at Toyota’s plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, in the US.
The battery supply chain will be spread across several locations, with Toyota stating that the battery modules for the Highlander will be assembled at its battery plant in North Carolina. The cells produced by LGES in Lansing can thus be further processed within a largely US-based supply chain before the battery is installed in the vehicle in Kentucky.
Unlike the Toyota cells, production of LFP cells for stationary energy storage systems is already underway in Lansing. LGES manufactures lithium iron phosphate cells there for so-called Energy Storage Systems (ESS). These will be integrated by the US subsidiary LG Energy Solution Vertech into complete systems for energy suppliers, as well as commercial and industrial applications. Among the future customers is the energy provider DTE Energy from Detroit.
Tesla to source cells from Lansing in 2027
Among other applications, the cells are expected to be used, among other applications, in Tesla’s Megapack 3, whose production is planned for Houston, Texas, in the US. This development means that, in addition to its business with EV batteries, LGES is increasingly tapping into the market for stationary large-scale storage systems.
This diversification is strategically significant for the Lansing site. What was originally a cell factory heavily tailored to General Motors’ ramp-up has evolved into a facility serving two distinct markets and cell chemistries: high-energy-density NMC cells for electric vehicles and more cost-effective, cycle-resistant LFP cells for stationary storage.
The different applications place distinct demands on the batteries. In vehicles, energy density, weight, and installation space are particularly critical. For stationary storage, however, the focus is primarily on costs, lifespan, and a high number of charge cycles.
LGES expands ESS business in North America
Lansing is also part of a broader strategy by LG Energy Solution. By the end of 2026, the company aims to establish over 50 GWh of production capacity for LFP cells for stationary storage across three of its own and two jointly operated sites in North America.
According to the group, around 80 per cent of its global ESS production capacity will then be located in North America. LGES is responding to both the growing demand for locally produced batteries and the increasing need for large-scale storage systems for power grids, renewable energy, and industrial applications.
What was once planned as the third Ultium plant for GM and LGES has thus become a significantly more diversified battery production site. Toyota secures part of the future demand from the automotive sector, while the ESS business already ensures capacity utilisation. For LGES, this combination also reduces dependence on the market ramp-up of individual electric vehicle models and manufacturers.

title: Exclusive: Is the Arctic set to be China’s new battery highway to Europe? – Batteries International
content: China is turning the Arctic into a new maritime highway for its battery and EV industries, opening a dramatically shorter route to European markets as conflict and disruption continue to plague traditional global shipping lanes. Chinese carrier Sea Legend has begun regularising its China-Europe Arctic Express, following a successful trial voyage last year carrying Chinese electric vehicles and other high-value manufactured goods through Russia’s Northern Sea Route. The attraction is speed. The Arctic passage can put cargo into northern Europe in around 20 days, compared with roughly 40 days through the Suez Canal and as much as 50 days when vessels are forced around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope. For battery manufacturers — particularly those shipping high-value lithium cells, battery packs and EV components — cutting several weeks from the journey could have significant implications for inventory, working capital and European supply chains. And what began as an experiment is becoming considerably more serious. Temperature control Sea Legend has scheduled eight consecutive weekly sailings from Ningbo-Zhoushan between August and October this year, deploying seven vessels compared with the single ship used for its 2025 trial. Russian  Information & Analytical Agency PortNews said on August 15 that Chinese lithium battery manufacturer EVE Energy will be among firms involved in some of the early shipments to test the transport chain for a small batch of power batteries, including temperature control and customs clearance, although Batteries International has not independently verified that report. Batteries International can also confirm that South Korea is also exploiting the new route to lucrative European markets, with that country’s PanStar line setting off on a pilot trip through the Arctic on or around August 22. PanStar has not disclosed detailed cargo inventories but confirmed it would be shipping “a wide range of products including automotive parts” on the voyage from Busan Port with subsequent onward journeys to Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Hamburg in Germany and Gdańsk in Poland. Asia’s Silk Road tributary through the normally frozen Arctic wastes is in part thanks to climate change, which has made the region more navigable at certain times of the year. Warm relations between Asian nations such as China and Russia — whose state-owned atomic energy corporation Rosatom is responsible for issuing shipping permits for the NSR — are also a major geopolitical factor. Environmental concerns The Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), the world’s largest container shipping line, has already ruled out operating any Asia-Europe services via the NSR. The announcement came as the China-Europe Arctic Express initiative was launched in 2025. MSC said while the NSR offered potential advantages — such as shorter transit times and lower fuel consumption — its stance underscored “risks and uncertainties” associated with the route, not least on environment and regulatory grounds. Batteries International has seen the first batch of sailing schedules for the China-Europe Arctic Express that were released by the China Shipowners’ Association on July 29. In addition to Sea Legend, voyages will be undertaken by China’s Xin Xin Shipping, Ningbo Hongkun Shipping, Dalian Trawind Shipping, Tianjin Yueqian Shipping and and Shanghai Dahua Shipping. According to the published schedules, participating operators plan to deploy around 20,000 teu (20 foot equivalent unit) of container ship and multi-purpose vessel capacity, together with around 1.4 million deadweight tonnes (DWT) of bulk carrier capacity. Sea Legend itself will run eight fixed weekly sailings though to early October, using seven vessels and targeting transit times of around 20 to 22 days. According to the China National Shipping Service (CNSS), cargo will include lithium ion batteries, photovoltaic products and new energy vehicle/EV components. Resilient supply chains CNSS said the move will shorten trips between Chinese ports and key Baltic gateways by around a third, as businesses seek more diversified and resilient supply chains amid rising risks along traditional maritime routes. The new service will consolidate cargo from multiple Chinese ports before calling at Ningbo-Zhoushan Port and sailing for Felixstowe in the UK, with connections to other European ports including Rotterdam, Netherlands, Wilhelmshaven in Germany, and Poland’s Gdynia. Industry calculations cited by CNSS claim the Arctic route can shorten the sailing distance on some Northeast Asia-Northern Europe services by around 30%-40%, compared with conventional seaways via the Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope. Sea Legend has deployed seven container vessels ranging from 1,384 teu to 4,890 teu. The first sailing, to be operated by the Dubai Tower, was scheduled to leave Ningbo on August 15 and arrive at Felixstowe on September 7. The Chinese Communist Party-backed Global Times claimed the Arctic’s “naturally low temperatures can be suitable for the transport of high-value goods such as energy-storage, helping reduce some temperature-related transport risks”. However, no firm scientific evidence was cited. PanStar general manager Kang Sang-in has said the Korean pilot voyage offered an opportunity to open a new chapter for the country’s shipping industry. “We have largely alleviated market concerns about the Arctic route, seeing it lead to actual bookings and confirming its commercial potential.” The pilot will comprehensively verify operational safety and business viability and lead to a review of potential regular services using the Arctic in the future. New energy vehicles China’s state Xinhua news agency reported in September 2025 that Sea Legend had tested the viability of faster Arctic shipping with a single voyage last year with cargo mainly comprising new energy vehicles, lithium batteries and photovoltaic products. The voyage from Ningbo-Zhoushan Port to Felixstowe was completed in around 20 days — despite reducing speed as a result of severe weather in the Norwegian Sea, Xinhua said. According to Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, growing trade between East Asia and Europe is providing another source of momentum. “As a rising share of China’s exports consists of higher-value advanced manufactured products, new Eurasian transport corridors have a stronger cargo base on which to develop.” Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, said traditional shipping routes still hold advantages in capacity, infrastructure and established networks, but rising geopolitical tensions had pushed up fuel and operating costs on some corridors, while tighter control over key ports had added to concerns over global shipping security. “Against this backdrop, developing alternative corridors and building a more diversified shipping network have become an increasingly necessary choice.” Gordon Chang, a distinguished senior fellow and member of the advisory board of the Gatestone Institute — a non-profit international policy council and think tank — said in analysis published on August 18: “For many reasons, the world’s biggest shipping companies do not sail the NSR. It is, for instance, not passable in winter, and even in summer ships can end up trapped in ice. “Moreover, Russia, after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has been heavily sanctioned and most companies do not want to deal with Rosatom, which issues permits for the NSR.” Marie-Caroline Laurent, group senior VP for maritime policy and government affairs at global container shipping company MSC, told the International Chamber of Shipping earlier this year that the firm would not use the NSR as a maritime trade route to transit the Arctic. “There are significant safety, environmental and social issues surrounding trans-Arctic shipping. These issues also raise questions of the operational viability and economic case for the use of the NSR. “While transit times may be reduced during a limited period of the year, any perceived gains are likely to be entirely outweighed by significantly higher costs, capacity restrictions, and the operational uncertainty inherent to the route — particularly due to heightened geopolitical tensions.” Sanctions complications Meanwhile, insurer Allianz Commercial said in its 2026 safety and shipping review that sanctions imposed on Russia after the invasion of Ukraine could complicate rescue efforts if a vessel gets into trouble in the Arctic and requires assistance. According to Allianz, the Arctic economy has tripled in size since 2003 to more than $650 billion, driven by resource extraction, trade route development and increased investment, particularly from Russia. Allianz analysis showed that machinery damage or failure was the cause of almost half of the 500+ reported shipping incidents in Arctic Circle waters over the past decade. title: Lead battery industry wins EU reprieve until 2030 – Batteries International
content: ILA has successfully lobbied for the transfer of restrictions affecting lead batteries from the EU’s end-of-life vehicles legislation, moving them into the Batteries Regulation. This substantial change means that the next review of the exemption allowing use of lead batteries in vehicles – which was scheduled to take place in 2025 – moves to the Batteries Regulation and will not take place before 2030. In addition, any future review of the exemption will take into consideration economic and social impacts as well as technical assessments. ILA, together with partners in EUROBAT, ACEA and JAMA have previously had to make a case every 3-5 years for continuation of the exemption of 12V lead batteries from the general prohibition on use of lead in vehicles that has applied for more than 20 years. They have also had to deal with the risk of restrictions or authorisation of use of lead in batteries through the REACH Regulation. Dr Steve Binks, ILA’s Senior Regulatory Affairs Director, welcomed the move, saying: “We identified that replacement of the existing ELV directive with a new regulation was an opportunity to simplify the EU legislative environment for lead batteries. In future the EU Battery Regulation will act as the focal point for decisions on hazardous substance restrictions in batteries and legislation such as REACH and ELV legislation become less relevant. “We delivered a coordinated advocacy campaign, supported by EUROBAT, engaging with key stakeholders in the EU parliament, member states, and the council of the EU to make a powerful case for the importance of lead batteries to the EU economy and society. We argued that the review of the exemption belongs in the Batteries Regulation and this had the benefit of pushing any future review of lead battery use in vehicles beyond 2030. Dr Binks, who will be briefing delegates at the ELBC conference in Vienna in September on the implications of the Batteries Regulation, added: “I think this highlights how important it is for industries like ours to demonstrate the strategically important contribution we make to growth, sustainability and economic resilience in Europe.” The council of the EU announced the formal adoption of the revised end-of-life vehicles regulation in June. It is expected to be published in the EU’s official journal in August, and will enter into force three weeks later. The regulation will start applying two years after its entry into force. title: Toyota RAV4 PHEV GR Sport Review And Analysis
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
The plug-in hybrid crossover achieves nearly 60 miles of electric driving in real-world tests, though cabin materials disappoint.
August 18, 2026
5 Min Read
The RAV4 plug-in hybrid poses with charging stations rather than gas pumps, though it can use both.
At a Glance
The RAV4 PHEV's 49-mile EPA rating extends to nearly 60 miles in mixed driving conditions.
GR Sport trim uses slower J1772 charging while other RAV4 PHEV models get faster CCS ports.
Suspension upgrades reduce friction and body roll, but cabin materials lag behind Hyundai and Kia.
RAV4 is such a hot property that some buyers are paying a premium over the sticker price, which, in the case of our GR Sport all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid, is already a substantial $51,335.
While paying extra is nuts, the RAV4 is an appealing option in the compact crossover category that it pioneered. Our Supersonic Red GR Sport, with its gloss black trim, struck a sporty figure that would surely be the envy of the elementary school drop-off line.
There’s a roof-mounted spoiler at the rear that helps smooth airflow off the back of the roof for reduced drag and improved highway efficiency. The test car also had the optional $320 crossbars on the roof rails. These are practical for hauling objects like bikes that don’t fit inside, and when there’s nothing mounted on them, they create the impression of two more roof-mounted spoilers, like some kind of serious rally racer.
As a plug-in hybrid, efficiency is the RAV4 GR Sport’s calling card. The EPA says that the 2.5-liter inline 4-cylinder engine and continuously variable transmission combine with an electric motor to produce a combined 320 horsepower while delivering an EPA-estimated 37 mpg in combined city and highway driving.
All RAV4 PHEVs enjoy an upgrade to silicon carbide semiconductors in the front axle’s power electronics. Along with the car’s larger battery, the plug-in RAV4 is now rated at 49 miles of electric-only driving range. The charging port on high-end XSE and Woodland models is a battery-electric style Combined Charge System port that supports DC fast charging and 11-kilowatt Level 2 AC charging.
Inexplicably, the tested GR Sport is fitted with a lesser J1772 Level 2 AC port only. There is no DC fast charging, and the AC charge rate is limited to 7 kW. A Toyota spokesman couldn’t explain why the GR Sport’s charging is handicapped compared to the other models, but did say that the company is listening to customer feedback about the difference in the charge ports and a possible switch to a single Tesla-style North American Charging Standard (NACS) charge port.
Charging is relevant even with the RAV4’s gas engine because, with its 49-mile EPA-rated driving range, the GR Sport can function as a battery electric vehicle during around-town driving. In mixed driving that included time at highway speed, the RAV4 consistently demonstrated the ability to go 10-15% further on its battery than the predicted electric range, boosting its EV driving distance to nearly 60 miles without switching to gas power.
Indeed, during a week of driving, the test car traveled 170 miles using only electricity. The RAV4’s gas engine never started during the whole week. As a result, it only cost $6.80 in electricity to drive that 170 miles. At $4/gallon, the 37-mpg RAV4 would burn $18.38 worth of gas to drive the same distance without the benefit of the plug-in battery charge, and a typical 20-mpg non-hybrid SUV would use $34 worth of gas. The math, as they say, ain’t mathin’ for combustion power here.
GR is Toyota’s brand that refers to Gazoo Racing, the company’s factory-backed racing team, so naturally, the GR Sport edition of the RAV4 enjoys some upgrades to its suspension. Engineers tweaked the RAV4’s coil springs to reduce friction, and the shocks get revised bushings, pistons, and oil, also to reduce friction in the system. More specific details were lost to the language barrier between the Japanese engineers and your English-only correspondent.
The GR Sport also has a thicker anti-sway bar to keep the car flatter in corners, and Toyota’s Vehicle Braking Posture Control system to further reduce vehicle roll by applying force to the front outer wheel and rear inner wheel in turns to stabilize the vehicle.
The result wouldn’t be mistaken for the handling of Toyota’s racy GR Corolla, but the RAV4 GR Sport is pleasant, competent, and comfortable enough to satisfy anyone who isn’t cross-shopping the Porsche Macan.
The RAV4 GR Sport gets exciting red trim, but the dashboard, console, and door panel materials look inexpensive in person. TOYOTA
What won’t withstand much scrutiny is the RAV4’s cabin, whose appointments are disappointingly cheap-looking. It isn’t that there is anything wrong. It is just that the many hard surfaces convey the impression of cost-cutting throughout. Anyone comparing it to products from Hyundai and Kia will find the material quality wanting.
What they might like, however, is the traditional sliding PRNDL shifter, which slides through all of the discrete positions of each gear selection rather than springing back to center and potentially leaving the driver unsure whether the intended gear has been selected. Toyota is ahead of its rivals here.
Lastly, there is the matter of the RAV4’s stereo system. There is a volume knob, which is good. But there is little incentive to twist it clockwise for more volume because the RAV4’s unbranded stereo is the worst-sounding factory audio system I can remember in years. It is boomy and unclear in its sound reproduction. While compact crossover buyers may be resigned to driving carpool, they might want to be able to enjoy their music while waiting curbside for practice to end, and in the RAV4 they’ll be tempted to resort to using their ear buds instead.
It should come as no surprise that the company that popularized hybrids in the US would build an exemplary plug-in hybrid. Just don’t overpay to get one. And consider splurging on a higher-grade audio system.

title: The Supply Chain Hero Award 2026 Shortlist: A Closer Look
content:
The Supply Chain Hero Award 2026 Shortlist: A Closer Look
Prioritise Us
on Google
The Global Supply Chain Awards is now less than a month away
As the Global Supply Chain Awards 2026 edge closer, we examine the individuals who have been shortlisted for The Supply Chain Hero Award
With September 8 fast approaching, we are excited to welcome leading supply chain innovators to the JW Marriott Grosvenor House London to celebrate the achievements in our sector.
One of the most anticipated categories of the night is
The Supply Chain Hero Award
, which will shine a light on some of the most talented contributors to logistics.
Sitting down to an exclusive gala dinner at this black-tie event, attendees will be able to hear the stories behind some of the most successful global supply chain networks.
Supply chain heroes honoured
The reason this award is one of the focal points of the awards celebration is clear. Behind every high-performing supply chain function are the individuals pushing for its success. Without these leaders, many functions would be left behind.
It has not been easy, navigating the turbulent and testing environment while aiming for seamless global operations in the current climate. With tariffs, trade routes blocked and
socioeconomic policies shifting
, organisations have had to be agile to react to these conditions.
Resilience is only one part; this honour will also be looking at the men and women who have shown exceptional commitment and leadership, as well as the problem-solving skills that have been so heavily relied on to sustain ongoing success.
Only the leaders showing the dedication to the function, which in turn will have had a significant and measurable impact on the success of their supply chain’s function, will have made
the shortlist
for this competitive category.
The Global Supply Chain Awards 2026 celebrates innovation and dedication
The judging criteria
Entries were measured against the following criteria:
Leadership qualities that have contributed towards measurable success
Tangible results that show the impact the individual has on the business
Demonstrable strategic and operational excellence
How the nominee fosters innovation and collaborates across teams
Who is on the shortlist this year?
Let’s take a look at who the judges deemed to have met this criteria.
Bhavik Pathak – Alstom
Prior to joining Alstom in 2021, Bhavik was a Commodity Manager / Strategic Sourcing, Major Systems & Key Suppliers Management at BOMBARDIER, a global leader in aviation and aerospace component manufacturing.
Now in his current role as Director and Head of Supplier Quality – Americas Region at Alstom, he leads supplier quality strategy and execution across the Americas Region. As a result, Bhavik is responsible for governing around 40 suppliers across more than 20 manufacturing and project sites.
Bhavik recently told Supply Chain Digital
that Alstom is shifting from cost-focused sourcing to AI-driven resilience, supplier collaboration and predictive risk management. “We are changing from a traditional buyer model or the supplier quality engineer model to more of a risk and value architect,” Bhavik says.
Frank McKay – Jabil
Frank McKay, Senior Vice President, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Jabil
Frank McKay leads an organisation of around 3,000 employees across the Americas, Europe and Asia in his role as Senior Vice President, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Jabil.
His team, which is responsible for the company’s supply chain,
procurement strategies
and execution, prioritises delivering an optimised end-to-end supply chain that delivers value to customers and enables growth.
In his tenure at Jabil, which spans almost three decades, Frank has held various positions, including Vice President, Procurement & Purchasing Services and Chief Procurement Officer, in which he spearheaded a global team whose objective was to make processes as efficient as possible.
Frank champions digital innovation and AI-driven procurement models to improve agility and visibility and represents Jabil at global industry forums, sharing his passion and knowledge for operations.
James Rosengren – Mars Inc.
James Rosengren, Global Supply Chain Lead for Value Creation and Sustainability at Mars Snacking
James began his journey at Mars more than three years ago, starting as Head of Logistics before progressing to his current role of Global Supply Chain Lead for Value Creation and Sustainability at Mars Snacking. Prior to Mars, James worked for The Kraft Heinz Company, where he served in various capacities, including Continuous Improvement Manager.
He described himself as an “energetic, articulate and personable supply chain leader”, with a continuous improvement approach. This relentless drive for growth is one of the key qualities judges will have been looking for.
His focus currently is network optimisation and end-to-end value chain transformation, where he works to lead teams through strategic decision-making, seeing an increase in profits and a positive environmental impact.
Óscar Luis Rego Prieto – TK Elevator
Óscar Luis Rego Prieto, EVP – Chief Procurement Officer for TK Elevator
Óscar’s career spans more than three decades in global procurement and supply chain, leading him to his current role as EVP – Chief Procurement Officer for TK Elevator. Behind the title, he manages a global team of 405 professionals and an expenditure of around $4.9bn.
Describing himself as a “creative and committed leader”, Óscar focuses on building high-performance teams capable of working effectively in functions like change management, strategic sourcing and
demand management
. As a result, he is respected by workers and board members alike.
Óscar has now been utilising his skillset at TK Elevator for the past five years, but before this, he also served as CPO for Constellium and CPO at Acciona Infrastructures.
Syed Moiz Ishaq – K-Electric
Syed Moiz Ishaq, Chief of Supply Chain at K-Electric (Image source: Syed Ishaq via LinkedIn)
With more than 22 years’ experience across the energy and manufacturing sectors, Syed is a leader who is passionate about building resilient, transparent, and data-driven supply chains.
He has been at K-Electric for over 15 years after first joining as a Deputy General Manager for Procurement in 2011 and has held multiple positions during this time, including Head of Procurement and Head of Inventory Management, Warehousing and Quality Assurance.
While working his way to his current role as Chief of Supply Chain, Syed has helped to drive digital transformation by strengthening governance frameworks and e-procurement. When looking at his leadership style, he says he “combines strategic thinking with operational execution”, which is helped by his commitment to developing talent, collaborating and his focus on continued improvement.
Winners will be revealed on 8 September LIVE at the Global Supply Chain Awards.

title: A Closer Look at the Enterprise of the Year Shortlist 2026
content:
A Closer Look at the Enterprise of the Year Shortlist 2026
Prioritise Us
on Google
A scene from the Global Procurement & Supply Chain Awards 2025
As the Global Supply Chain Awards are mere weeks away, we take a closer look at the leaders shortlisted for the Enterprise of the Year Award 2026
With only a few weeks to go, leaders are eagerly anticipating the Global Supply Chain Awards, hosted at JW Marriott Grosvenor House London on 8 September.
At the exclusive black-tie event, leaders will be brought together to celebrate excellence and shine a light on emerging talents.
As the date nears, Supply Chain Digital takes a closer look at
those shortlisted
for the Enterprise of the Year Award.
Enterprise of the Year
Enterprise of the Year Award
provides recognition to organisations with more than 1,000 employees. Those recognised have proven themselves as influencers, setting new benchmarks and gaining strong results amid today's turbulent world.
This award has an all-encompassing criteria, so it may go to an enterprise that has demonstrated innovation, exceptional leadership in the sector or ongoing supply chain management success.
In the past few years, organisations have faced a series of challenges, with ongoing turbulence meaning leaders are having to think fast to adapt to fast-changing demands. The best enterprises have not only achieved this, but excelled in it.
The award is a great way to celebrate those organisations who are using innovative measures for good, using new strategies to make a difference and unlock new levels of success.
Join us at the Global Supply Chain Awards
Award criteria
Our judges had a strong set of criteria for this award, looking at:
Measurable impact across resilience, efficiency and innovation
Demonstrable consistency across supply chain management
How collaborative it has been across departments and partners
The wider influence on industry standards or practices
The shortlist
Outstanding entries from other categories have also been considered for this award.
JUSDA Supply Chain Management International Co., Ltd.
JUSDA is one of the shortlisted entries for Enterprise of the Year. Credit: JUSDA
JUSDA is a global supply chain management provider, using more than 20 years of expertise from managing Foxconn's lean supply chain. It helps a range of industries with supply chain transformation, being able to offer end-to-end solutions from raw material sourcing to final product delivery.
JUSDA uses AI and IoT to support organisations on their logistics journey, with services including truck, air and ocean transportation. It aims to optimise operations, drive efficiency and foster collaboration across the supply chain.
Mars is working towards recyclable packaging for its products to boost circularity. Credit: Mars
As a global company with a major footprint,
is the enterprise behind some of the world's favourite food, snacks and petcare. It is a family-owned organisation, dedicated to leaving a positive lasting impact on the world. It is constantly thinking about the future of its organisation, as well as what it can do for the community and the environment.
It operates on five principles, guiding and uniting the brands across its portfolio. That way, it is always striving for greatness, working towards constant improvement and accountability.
MISUMI Americas
MISUMI Americas acts as one source for all mechanical parts. Credit: MISUMI Americas
The sourcing partner for mechanical components helps across engineering, supply chain, procurement and manufacturing.
MISUMI Americas
helps organisations move from concept to production faster, using a range of AI-powered sourcing, digital tools, engineering expertise and a
reliable global supply chain
Through this, the manufacturing company drives scalability and innovation across every element of the supply chain, alongside reducing complexity.
Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc
Regeneron is working to bring new medicines to the market. Credit: Regeneron
Regeneron operates across an expanding global network to bring life-transforming medicines to those who need them. It aims to use scientific breakthroughs and innovation to repeatedly bring new medicines into the world, pushing the boundaries of discovery.
Using data-powered insights and pioneering genetic medicine platforms, the company is working to make a better future, alongside its efforts to divert waste from landfill.
TK Elevator
TK Elevator aims to make life more accessible. Credit: TK Elevator
TK Elevator is a pioneer in manufacturing, blending innovation, safety and reliability to create strong solutions. It operates across elevators, escalators, walkways, residential lifts and passenger boarding bridges, ensuring precision and efficiency at all times.
Sustainability is at the centre of its business model, as well as focusing on making life more accessible and more livable for people around the world.
Winners will be announced LIVE at the Awards Ceremony on 8 September.

title: Walmart: Embedding Sustainability Throughout Supply Chain
content:
Walmart: Embedding Sustainability Throughout Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Walmart is working to make its operations and supply chains more sustainable. Credit: Walmart
Walmart's 2026 ESG report explores how the organisation is driving operational resilience, efficiency and sustainability across its supply chain
Walmart operates more than 10,900 stores and serves approximately 280 million customers each week. According to the company's FY2026
ESG Report,
procurement networks and logistics operations form the basis of its approach to reducing emissions and managing environmental performance across global value chains.
The retailer generated US$713.2bn in revenue across 19 countries during the reporting period, supported by approximately 2.1 million associates. The scale of its purchasing operations could mean that decisions about sourcing, manufacturing standards and supplier engagement influence practices across entire commodity sectors.
Everyday Resilience: protecting communities and supporting recovery in times of disaster
Supplier networks and emissions reduction
Walmart states that procurement relationships are central to its strategy for managing emissions beyond direct operations. The company uses purchasing decisions to encourage suppliers to adopt lower-carbon manufacturing processes, reduce packaging and improve transparency across production networks.
According to the report, suppliers engaged through Project Gigaton have reported initiatives expected to avoid, reduce or sequester 1.37 billion tonnes of CO₂e through 2030. These projects were implemented since 2017 and focus on manufacturing emissions, logistics, energy use and agricultural practices.
"Suppliers engaged through our Project Gigaton platform reported projects since 2017 expected to avoid, reduce or sequester 1.37 billion tonnes of CO₂e through 2030," says Kathleen McLaughlin, Executive Vice President and Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart, in the report.
Kathleen McLaughlin, Executive Vice President and Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart Inc
The platform provides tools for tracking emissions reductions and sharing best practices across manufacturing networks.
The retailer aligns its emissions reporting with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and receives third-party assurance for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. The report states that climate resilience depends on addressing emissions from manufacturing, logistics and agricultural supply chains, recognising that most retail emissions occur beyond direct operations.
Procurement standards and commodity chains
The FY2026 report states that supplier engagement extends beyond emissions measurement. According to the company, stakeholders prioritise supply chain transparency, responsible recruitment, ocean health, deforestation prevention and
packaging reduction
Walmart completed its decade-long 20x25 initiative, which sought to improve environmental and social sustainability across 20 global commodity value chains by 2025. The programme focused on commodity reporting, certification systems and traceable sourcing for products including timber, seafood and agricultural goods.
Manufacturing sustainability
is supported through programmes designed to encourage regenerative agriculture, sustainable packaging and improved labour practices throughout production networks. The company provides development programmes, marketplace tools and responsible sourcing initiatives to support suppliers in meeting environmental and social standards.
Walmart Manufacturing leverages innovation and cutting-edge technology. Credit: Walmart
What is the Greenhouse Gas Protocol?
The Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHG Protocol) is the world's most widely used global standardised framework for measuring, managing and reporting greenhouse gas emissions.
Created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), it divides emissions into three clear categories: Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3.
The report states that embedding sustainability requirements into supplier relationships and procurement decisions could improve resilience while reducing environmental impacts. Walmart measures waste, food waste and packaging using recognised international methodologies, including Zero Waste International Alliance principles and the Food Loss and Waste Standard.
Operations and renewable energy sourcing
Walmart achieved its target of sourcing 50% of electricity from renewable sources in FY2026.
"In our operations, we reached our targets of sourcing 50% of our electricity from renewable sources, and we have reduced our absolute Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 24.6% compared with our 2015 baseline year (achieving a 53.7% reduction in emissions intensity over the same period)," adds Kathleen.
The company states that reducing operational emissions supports more resilient infrastructure and lowers costs. Energy transition remains a priority, with
renewable energy procurement
forming part of the strategy to reduce Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.
Walmart and the Walmart Foundation have an ambitious strategy to protect and replenish biodiversity. Credit: Walmart
What is the Zero Waste International Alliance?
It's a global network founded in 2003 that promotes zero waste practices, sets official industry definitions and guides communities and businesses away from landfills and incineration.
Beyond its own facilities, the retailer continues to work with suppliers to reduce emissions from manufacturing and logistics networks. The report explains that decarbonising retail operations requires collaboration across value chains, with suppliers playing a role in implementing emissions reduction projects.
Governance structures ensure ESG priorities influence decision making throughout the organisation. According to the report, executive leadership and board committees oversee sustainability initiatives, rather than confining responsibility to specialist teams.
Technology supports Walmart's approach to
managing supply chain operations
and improving environmental performance. The company describes itself as a "people-led, tech-powered" omnichannel business that uses digital capabilities to strengthen operations and sustainability across value chains.
What is the Food Loss and Waste Standard?
This standard is a global rulebook that provides a common language, definitions and requirements for measuring and reporting the weight of food and inedible parts removed from the supply chain.
"Walmart was built on a simple idea: Help people save money and live better," says John Furner, President and CEO of Walmart, in the report.
"That purpose still guides us today as a people-led, tech powered omnichannel retailer serving millions of customers around the world each week.
"We must invest in our associates, building skills for the future. We help our suppliers and sellers reach new markets and grow their businesses. Through our people and technology, we are enhancing the sustainability of our operations and our value chains. And every day we focus on using our strengths to build the resilience of communities we serve."
John Furner, Walmart CEO (Credit: Walmart)
The report states that responsible
use of data and AI
forms part of the ESG governance framework. Walmart completed its five-year commitment to invest US$1bn in associate education and training, preparing employees for technology-enabled roles.
According to the company, approximately 86% of above-entry-level US positions were filled internally during FY2026. Skills development could support both employee retention and operational resilience as automation and digital tools become more common across retail and logistics operations.
Walmart donated 769 million pounds of food in the US during FY2026 and provided US$1.97bn in global cash and in-kind community contributions. The report states that delivering sustainability at global scale requires addressing emissions, supporting workforce development and managing social impacts across supply chains.

title: Lucid unveils its 2027 Air EV lineup with a new Stealth package
content:
Lucid unveiled its 2027 Air lineup, streamlining the options across its electric sedan range and adding a new Stealth & Sound Package for the entry-level Air Pure.
The Air Grand Touring keeps its title as the longest-range EV on sale at up to 512 miles, and pricing holds flat across all four trims for the new model year.
What’s new for 2027
The biggest change is in the configurator, not the car. Lucid says the 2027 pricing guides “reflect a more focused set of available options for Air Pure,” trimming the entry model’s long à la carte menu down to a tighter set of choices.
The centerpiece is a new Stealth & Sound Package for the Air Pure, priced at $6,250, that bundles the most popular options into a single configuration. Buyers who add it can pick either 19-inch Aero Range Stealth or 20-inch Aero Lite Stealth wheels, plus a paint finish in Infinite Black Metallic, Stellar White Metallic, or Quantum Grey Metallic.
The Touring, Grand Touring, and Sapphire carry into 2027 largely as they were. The whole lineup is configurable now through Lucid’s Design Yours tool.
Prices hold flat across the lineup
Every trim keeps its 2026 starting price for the new model year, in both the US and Canada. That’s worth a note in 2026: tariffs on imported vehicles and parts have pushed costs up across the industry, and the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September 2025, so effective EV prices have been climbing. Lucid left the Air’s sticker alone.
Top comment by Beario
While I like Lucid and wish them success, this year and early next year will be important for them with the release of the Gravity model. Not taking anything away from an updated Air, but it would have been great if Lucid had laid out a roadmap filled with more vehicles like Rivian did when they introduced the R2, R3, and R3X but even one more Lucid model gives hope that they can last and be profitable to build more cars down the road.
Here’s the lineup, 2026 versus 2027:
| Air | 2026 US | 2027 US | 2026 Canada | 2027 Canada | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pure | $70,900 | $70,900 | CA$99,900 | CA$99,900 | No change |
| Touring | $79,900 | $79,900 | CA$112,800 | CA$112,800 | No change |
| Grand Touring | $114,900 | $114,900 | CA$161,200 | CA$161,200 | No change |
| Sapphire | $249,000 | $249,000 | CA$327,300 | CA$327,300 | No change |
It helps that the Air is selling well at the top of its class. We reported last year that the Air became the best-selling luxury EV sedan in the US, passing Tesla’s Model S. And the range crown isn’t just an EPA number — the Air won Norway’s brutal EV winter test earlier this year, a real-world result that’s harder to argue with than a lab figure.
However, the focus for Lucid has been on the Gravity this year and it is showing in this lack of change with the 2027 model year.

title: Here's our first look at the new Hyundai Tucson inside and out [Images]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 19 2026 - 7:55 am PT
revealed the exterior and interior design of the all-new Tucson for the first time, and it already looks like a big upgrade.
Meet the new Hyundai Tucson
It’s been six years since Hyundai launched the current fourth-generation Tucson. For the fifth-gen model, Hyundai is taking the SUV to the next level.
The new Hyundai Tucson has grown up and now looks more like a traditional SUV, with a wide, boxy stance.
The new look is based on Hyundai’s “Art of Steel” design, the same design philosophy behind the off-road Boulder Concept from the New York Auto Show earlier this year.
Hyundai’s bold off-road-like design is becoming its signature, similar to the new look that Kia has created over the past few years.
Up front, the redesigned Tucson features new vertical “H-edge” daytime running lights and a slim horizontal light bar. Hyundai said the lights in the bar are not directly exposed on the outside, helping to create the bold, three-dimensional look.
The new Hyundai Tucson (Source: Hyundai)
The rear features a prism rear lamp with a three-dimensional protruding lens structure. When illuminated, the lamp is revealed, adding “visual three-dimensionality.”
The new Hyundai Tucson measures 4,700 mm (185″) long, 1,905 mm (75″) wide, and 1,685 mm (66″) high, with a 2,785 mm (110″) wheelbase.
The new Hyundai Tucson (Source: Hyundai)
Compared to the current model, the new Tucson is 60 mm longer, 40 mm wider, and has a 40 mm longer wheelbase. The increased dimensions open up “best-in-class interior space,” according to Hyundai.
The interior is fully redesigned, with a new floating structure to open up space and a large center infotainment screen.
New Hyundai Tucson interior (Source: Hyundai)
Hyundai equipped the new Tucson with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system. The setup includes a large center display with apps and customizable screens, plus a slim driver display.
The new Tucson will be available with Hyundai’s XRT trim, which adds to the rugged, off-road design. Added design elements include an exclusive front grille, wheels, and skid plates, black wheel arch garnishes, and XRT badging.
The new Hyundai Tucson and Tucson XRT (Source: Hyundai)
Inside, the Tucson XRT features exclusive patterned seats, dark metal decor, and protective floor mats for the first and second rows.
Hyundai has yet to reveal powertrain details, but like the current Tucson, the new version is expected to be sold as a hybrid and plug-in hybrid, not pure electric.
While the Tucson likely won’t be offered with a fully electric powertrain, Hyundai still offers the
, which is about the same size. We will have to wait until closer to launch for the full details.

title: VMAX VX2 Lite review: Power and full suspension fun without the heavyweight price
content:
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Aug 19 2026 - 7:35 am PT
Electric scooters have long demonstrated an interesting dichotomy. On one end of the spectrum, you’ve got cheap commuter scooters that feel like they’re one pothole away from shaking themselves apart. On the other end are increasingly large, dual-motor monsters that weigh 80 or 100 pounds (45 kg) and blur the line between scooter and motorcycle.
The VMAX VX2 Lite aims for the sweet spot in the middle. It promises a genuine full-suspension ride, respectable 25 mph (40 km/h) performance, and up to 56 miles (90 km) of claimed range without turning into something you dread carrying up a flight of stairs. After spending time riding the long-range version, I think VMAX got surprisingly close to that goal.
I’ll tell you all about my experience riding the VMAX VX2 Lite electric scooter below, but why not also see it in action? Check out my review video here, then keep reading for all of my complete thoughts.
Suspension is the real star of the show
The biggest selling point here is undoubtedly the suspension.
The VX2 Lite combines a 47 mm hydraulic front fork with an elastomer rear suspension, and while that spec sheet doesn’t sound particularly exciting, it completely changes how the scooter feels to ride.
Instead of constantly bracing for cracks in the pavement or rough patches of asphalt, you simply ride through them. Expansion joints, brick streets, uneven bike paths, and rough pavement all become significantly less jarring.
And while the scooter is definitely not an off-roader, I specifically took it through some grass and dirt sections just to see how it fared. The street tires aren’t really optimized for it, but the scooter handled dry off-road sections just fine.
More importantly, that suspension doesn’t just make a scooter more comfortable – it makes it more fun. There’s a weird child-like thrill from purposefully ramping off of speed bumps when you know the landing is going to be controlled and not shake your ankle bones out of position.
I found myself taking routes I might normally avoid simply because the scooter handled rough surfaces so much better. The tires stay planted, the steering feels calmer, and the overall ride inspires more confidence. It transforms the experience from cautiously avoiding imperfections to simply enjoying the ride.
That’s a hard thing to appreciate from a spec sheet, but it’s immediately obvious once you’re rolling.
Surprisingly punchy performance
The other pleasant surprise was the motor.
On paper, the VX2 Lite uses a 500W nominal rear hub motor with up to 1,400W peak output. The continuous power number off 500W doesn’t necessarily scream performance, but the scooter feels much stronger than I expected. That’s the peak power speaking. And to really make use of that peak power, you’ll want to put the scooter in Beast Mode (five quick pushes on the power button and then one push of the throttle). For some people, that may even be more power than they need, but if you can handle it, it’s a lot of fun to have that much acceleration underneath you.
Don’t worry though, if you just leave it in normal mode then you’re still getting a lot of the scooter, plus you’ll have the benefit of even longer range – but more on that soon.
Acceleration is brisk enough to keep city riding entertaining, and I never found myself wishing for significantly more power during normal urban riding. I don’t have a ton of hills to test out in my flat city, but climbing parking garage ramps and other short steep ramps definitely showed off the power hiding away in this scooter. VMAX’s claimed ability to climb grades up to 28% isn’t something I could test myself (most people don’t have any 28% grade hills in their area – that’s some serious incline), but it also doesn’t seem unrealistic for shorter climbs, based on what I experienced.
The 25 mph (40 km/h) top speed also feels like a nice balance. It’s quick enough to comfortably keep pace with urban traffic in many situations without venturing into the “this is getting a little ridiculous” territory occupied by some high-performance scooters.
Even on the crazy super scooters that can hit twice these speeds or more, I rarely like going much faster than 40 mph (64 km/h), and even that feels a bit reckless unless the wheels are huge. Here, 25 mph (40 km/h) seems sensibly fast, especially since people rarely use the absolute top speed of a scooter anyway. And with 10″ tires, these are actually larger wheels than you’ll find on a lot of budget scooters, so you have a bit more confidence at these speeds, too.
A commuter that feels well thought out
Little design decisions often separate good scooters from great ones, and VMAX deserves credit for getting a lot of those details right.
One of my favorites is the folding latch. After unfolding the scooter, the latch folds neatly down against the deck and locks itself out of the way. It sounds like a tiny feature, but anyone who’s ever had a folding latch poking into their foot while riding will immediately appreciate it.
I saw it on the VX2 Hub also
, a faster and more powerful big brother to the VX2 Lite, and it’s a neat little feature.
The folding mechanism in the stem also feels reassuringly solid. There’s no discernible play once locked into position, giving the scooter a sturdy, confidence-inspiring feel.
VMAX has long made good lighting a priority on its electric scooters, complete with deck and bar-mounted turn signals
Lighting is another highlight.
The VX2 Lite doesn’t settle for a basic headlight and tiny rear reflector. Instead, it includes bright lighting all around, complete with motorcycle-style turn signals integrated into both the deck and the ends of the handlebars. They’re much more visible than the tiny blinking indicators found on many scooters, and anything that makes riders more noticeable to drivers gets a thumbs-up from me.
Again, this is par for the course with VMAX, as I’ve enjoyed this well-designed wraparound lighting with highly visible turn signals
on several of the company’s models before
. It’s an important part of riding, especially at night when you’re basically just a narrow vertical stick on two wheels, compared to cars looking for other cars.
Thank you for not forcing an app
This is becoming one of my biggest pet peeves in the micromobility industry.
Too many companies now expect riders to download an app, create an account, pair the scooter, verify an email address, and usually even accept privacy policies before they can access basic functions.
Thankfully, VMAX didn’t go down that road.
The companion app exists if you want additional ride data and customization, but you don’t need it.
Power modes, riding settings, and normal operation can all be handled directly from the scooter itself. And to prevent having too many buttons, several features (like opening and locking that Beast Mode) are performed by the same button, just with different numbers of quick presses.
Not requiring an app might sound like a small thing, but I genuinely appreciate products that still function perfectly well without requiring me to download another app onto my phone.
It’s just how these vehicles should work.
Weight and value
At around 52 lb (23.6 kg) for the larger battery version I tested, or 48 lb (21.8 kg) for the smaller battery version, I wouldn’t call the VX2 Lite lightweight. You’ll still notice it if you’re carrying it upstairs every day.
But context matters here. Compared to many other full-suspension scooters with similar ride quality and performance, it’s actually fairly light. VMAX has done a nice job balancing portability with comfort, and I think they landed in a reasonable place.
Pricing is another pleasant surprise.
The lineup starts at
$799 for the 499 Wh version
with a claimed 31-mile range, while the larger 874 Wh battery model I tested
comes in at $1,099
. In today’s market, that’s a pretty competitive starting price for a scooter that delivers this level of refinement, suspension, and performance.
Sure, there are cheaper models from a never-ending list of Chinese companies, and I’m not knocking them, but you do feel a real difference in the quality and ride of a VMAX scooter. So in this case, you get what you pay for – and I still think the price is fair. Add in the included 2-year warranty, which twice what the budget brands usually offer, and it looks even better.
And with reasonable pricing, you get to save some cash for extra accessories. I tested out the folding lock from VMAX, and it’s a convenient way to carry a small lock in a holster on the scooter itself, but that still opens up into a large circle for locking to non-standard racks, small trees, etc. But they’ve got tons of
other accessories
worth checking out, also.
A couple of things I’d still change
No product is perfect, and the VX2 Lite isn’t an exception.
My biggest complaint is simply that I’d always prefer a scooter to weigh less. While it’s lighter than many competitors in this category, 50-ish pounds is still enough that you’ll think twice before carrying it long distances.
The other nitpick is cosmetic.
The available colorway is clean and understated, but it doesn’t exactly stand out. To be fair, most electric scooter manufacturers seem convinced that buyers only want black scooters, so VMAX isn’t exactly alone here. Still, a splash of color would have been nice. But then again, a black canvas does give you plenty of open real estate to play around with your own coloring, stickers, or however you want to customize your ride.
Final thoughts
The VMAX VX2 Lite manages to do something I always appreciate: it avoids chasing spec-sheet bragging rights and instead focuses on making the riding experience better.
The suspension genuinely improves both comfort and fun. The motor feels stronger than its rating suggests. The thoughtful design touches make everyday use easier. And perhaps most refreshing of all, it works perfectly well without demanding you install another smartphone app just to ride it.
If you’re shopping for a commuter scooter in the $800-$1,100 range and your priorities are ride quality, comfort, visibility, and solid real-world performance rather than outrageous top speeds, the VX2 Lite deserves a spot near the top of your list.
Sometimes, making a scooter more enjoyable isn’t about adding another motor or another 10 mph. Sometimes it’s simply about making every mile feel smoother and
. The VX2 Lite is a great example of exactly that.

title: Ex-Tesla president: Roadster delay is about getting closer to SpaceX ahead of merger
content:
Tesla Roadster
New Tesla Roadster
Fred Lambert
| Aug 19 2026 - 6:40 am PT
A former Tesla president says the endlessly delayed next-generation Roadster is being held up by SpaceX “hovering” technology — and that the project is really about pulling Tesla and SpaceX closer together.
Jon McNeill, Tesla’s president from 2015 to 2018 and now co-founder of VistaShares and CEO of DVx Ventures, made the comments as Tesla preps a long-promised Roadster demo nearly nine years after the car was first unveiled.
What the ex-president said
Speaking about the upcoming demonstration, McNeill said the event could show off the car’s most extreme party trick.
“I don’t know if we’re going to see flying, but we may see hovering in this demo,” he said via
McNeill framed the Roadster as a morale play for a company under pressure. “Elon recognizes that Tesla needs to inject some energy and excitement back into the car business,” he said.
He was more direct about the strategic motive. McNeill called the Roadster a “probably not-so-hidden attempt to further knit Tesla and SpaceX’s futures together,” and predicted the two companies “are going to come together, probably sooner rather than later.”
The “hovering” comes from a SpaceX-developed cold-gas thruster system, internally code-named A71, that points toward the ground to lift the car. We reported last week that Tesla’s
“flying” Roadster demo could happen this month
— and that the car would be remotely operated with no one inside, in part because the thrusters are loud enough to damage the hearing of anyone nearby.
A car promised in 2017 — and delayed at least nine times
Tesla unveiled the new Roadster in November 2017 with production promised for 2020. The reservation program asked buyers to put down up to $50,000, and Founders Series buyers wired the full $250,000.
The original specs were: a claimed 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed above 250 mph, and a 620-mile range — numbers that made it, on paper, the quickest production car ever announced. None of it required rocket thrusters.
The SpaceX package came later, as an add-on Elon Musk teased would cut the 0-60 time to roughly 1.1 seconds using cold-gas thrusters. Since then, the car has been
delayed at least nine times
. The demo alone has slipped from April 1, 2026, to late April, to “maybe in a month” on the Q1 earnings call, to August 2026 — and now the thruster work is the reason it isn’t ready.
Even the demo has been scaled back. Earlier plans reportedly had the car racing up a magnetized ramp, driving upside down, righting itself, and hovering. Those elements were cut after being presented to Musk, who said about the demo “will be hard to pull off and could go wrong, but that it will be entertaining either way.”
The financial backdrop
The timing matters. TSLA is down roughly 25% year-to-date, the worst performer among the “Magnificent Seven,” and Tesla’s core auto business has been shrinking as competition intensifies. The full history of the program is tracked in our
Tesla Roadster guide
McNeill’s read that the Roadster is meant to “inject some energy and excitement” and knit Tesla and SpaceX together lands against that backdrop of a struggling car business and open speculation about a Tesla-SpaceX combination.
Electrek’s Take
Let’s be clear about what this is: a demo. That’s likely all it’s going to be.
It may well be true that the SpaceX cold-air thruster work is what’s holding up the Roadster, but if that’s the case, it’s bad business. The Roadster Tesla unveiled in 2017 was extremely well received. It didn’t have thrusters from SpaceX, and it didn’t need them. A 1.9-second 0-60, 250-plus mph, and a 620-mile range was already the most exciting car anyone had announced. No one who put down $50,000 was asking for cold-gas rockets that make the car undriveable and un-street-legal. Nobody is asking for that.
Tesla should just deliver the car it showed nearly nine years ago – hopefully with some upgrades since it has been a decade. Instead, the company is bolting on a gimmick with almost no real-world utility so it can stage a driverless “hovering” stunt in a Texas field.
And McNeill might be right about tying Tesla and SpaceX closer together ahead of a potential merger that would primarily benefit a single shareholder. Using a highly anticipated, long-overdue product as a prop for that agenda, when you had a great car to begin with, is pathetic. Deliver the Roadster people actually paid for, and do it 8 years ago. The rocket show can wait, and you don’t even need it. Elon can force anything he wants on Tesla shareholders and they will say thank you. History has proven that time and time again.

title: Study finds arable crops adapt surprisingly well to agrivoltaic shading - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A study by the University of Hohenheim found that barley, maize, cabbage, potatoes, and field beans can adapt their photosynthesis to partial shading in agrivoltaic systems. The findings suggest greater shade tolerance than previously assumed, although the physiological adaptations do not necessarily result in higher yields.
Ralph Diermann
19 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Utility-scale
The study shows that plants’ light requirements decrease significantly under partial shading.
How do crops such as barley, beans, potatoes, cabbage, and maize cope when photovoltaic modules reduce the sunlight reaching them? Better than previously thought, according to a study by Germany’s University of Hohenheim and the Jülich Research Centre. The crops are able to effectively adapt their photosynthesis to altered light conditions. The same applies to agroforestry systems, where trees or shrubs grow alongside crops on the same land.
The study found that the plants’ light requirements decrease significantly under partial shade. This allows them to use CO₂ more efficiently for photosynthesis despite reduced solar radiation. The researchers aim to use this adaptability to identify and breed crop varieties suitable for agrivoltaic systems.
“Greater adaptability than previously assumed”
For the study, the research team planted crops commonly grown in Germany — barley (
Hordeum vulgare
), maize (
Zea mays
), cabbage (
Brassica oleracea
), potatoes (
Solanum tuberosum
), and field beans (
Vicia faba
) — at five locations across the country and installed photovoltaic modules above them. Fully sunlit reference plots served as a basis for comparison. Using a mobile photosynthesis measurement system, the researchers recorded key physiological parameters directly from the leaves.
The most significant finding was that both dark respiration and the light compensation point decreased across all the crops studied under shaded conditions. “Put simply, this means the plants lost less CO₂ through respiration while simultaneously requiring less light to fix the carbon needed for growth and fruit production,” explained lead author Jennifer Moore. This demonstrates clear physiological adaptation to partial shade.
According to co-author Andreas Schweiger, it is particularly noteworthy that the effect occurred in all the crops studied, even though they typically do not grow in shaded conditions. “They possess a significantly greater capacity for adaptation than we previously assumed,” the scientist says.
These adaptations occurred regardless of location, soil type, farming method, or shading conditions. “Arable crops do not necessarily reach their limits under moderate shading; instead, they are able to adjust their metabolic activity,” says Schweiger.
Agrivoltaics can mitigate heat and drought stress
Physiological parameters such as dark respiration and the light compensation point could be used in the future to identify more shade-tolerant varieties and select them for cultivation systems involving partial shade. “Our findings help in the more targeted planning of agroforestry and agri-photovoltaic systems,” says Schweiger. Knowing which crops can maintain productivity under specific light conditions could help better match crop varieties with land-use systems. The researchers also see new opportunities for plant breeding.
The research team believes agrivoltaic systems could play an important role in helping agriculture adapt to climate change. They can mitigate heat and drought stress by improving the microclimate, lowering soil temperatures, and helping soil retain moisture for longer periods.
“In the face of climate change, periods of extreme heat and drought are likely to limit plant growth more severely than the shade cast by agroforestry or agri-photovoltaic installations,” says plant ecologist Schweiger. Consequently, the physiological adaptability of crops could become increasingly important in the future.
At the same time, the researchers emphasize that the observed physiological adaptations do not automatically translate into higher yields. Yield data varied depending on the location and crop type, with no uniform pattern emerging. The study therefore primarily provides fundamental insights into the mechanisms by which crops respond to natural shading.
The research work was presented in “
Partial shade effects of dual land use systems: Harnessing plant acclimation to drive sustainable farming solutions
,” published in the
European Journal of Agronomy

title: Megasol equips its solar panels with anti-glare surface - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Swiss manufacturer has made its ZRM+ anti-glare surface a standard feature across all Level Up solar roof modules. The microstructured glass reduces glare while maintaining a matte finish and the system’s technical performance.
François Puthod
19 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Since the launch of Level Up modules series in November 2025, shortly after the introduction of ZRM+ in the M450 roof module line, Swiss PV manufacturer
has received numerous customer requests to make anti-glare technology a standard feature of its roof modules.
Glare-free operation is particularly important for projects in densely populated residential areas or near transport routes, as well as for installations requiring permits in sensitive zones.
Megasol has responded by making ZRM+ technology standard rather than an optional feature. All Level Up modules will now be supplied exclusively with an anti-glare surface.
Proven effectiveness
Zero Reflect Matt+ (ZRM+) is a microstructured glass surface developed by Megasol that is designed to minimize disruptive glare. While conventional solar glass can produce strong reflections at unfavorable angles of incidence, the luminance of ZRM+ remains between 3,000 and 18,000 cd/m² at steep angles of incidence, according to Megasol. The company says this is comparable to the luminance of clay roof tiles. At an angle of incidence of 70°, luminance is approximately 29,000 cd/m², according to the manufacturer.
The effectiveness of ZRM+ has also been independently assessed. A glare report from the Bern University of Applied Sciences found luminance levels below the stated legal limit of 20,000 cd/m² across the tested angles of solar incidence, according to Megasol. The company therefore says the ZRM+ surface keeps glare outside the critical range regardless of the sun’s position.
Megasol said Level Up module is the first fully integrated solar roofing system to offer this anti-glare performance as a standard feature across the entire system, including the mounting system, rails and accessories.
The ZRM+ surface gives Level Up modules a deep matte finish, with the glass featuring a uniform, velvety appearance. According to Megasol, the system combines this aesthetic quality with frameless glass-glass modules, an efficiency of more than 200 Wp/m², hail resistance to Class 5 and rain tightness in accordance with CEN/TR 15601.

title: Ensuring safety of plug-in solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Plug-in (balcony) solar is a low-cost, plug-and-play alternative to traditional rooftop PV, gaining traction in the U.S. as states adopt legislation exempting small systems from interconnection requirements. Most states cap systems at 1,200 W and require UL 3700 safety certification, addressing risks such as circuit overload, electric shock and GFCI compatibility while costs and payback periods remain attractive.
Anne Fischer
19 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Residential
United States
Plug-in solar, also known as “balcony solar” is a new category of small, portable solar system that plugs directly into a wall outlet.
The concept took off in Germany in the 2010s with more than
one million plug-in solar devices
now registered. With ten U.S. states having adopted plug-in solar legislation with more to come, it’s beginning to take off in the U.S. as well. State legislation has many commonalities including interconnection exemption, wattage limits and safety certification.
While plug-in solar can still be used in states that have not passed legislation, potential users may have to apply to the local utility for interconnection approval. Most state legislation exempts the small systems from required interconnection agreements and approvals, which eliminates permitting and interconnection delays and associated fees.
Most state legislation has other similarities, for example, a wattage limit. Most have set a wattage limit of 1,200, although Colorado is the outlier, allowing systems of up to 1,920 watts, according to Bright Saver, a non-profit organization that sells plug-in solar kits.
UL 3700 safety certification is also required by most states, although Maine, New York and Vermont require that the inverter, panels, cables and mounting hardware all meet UL 3700 (or a comparable standard). According to Bright Saver, no vendor in the industry has achieved that yet.
UL 3700 was published in late 2025 and provides construction, performance and labeling criteria for plug-in solar systems. It is now the basis for UL Solutions’ safety testing and certification program for plug-in photovoltaic systems to which manufacturers can submit their systems for evaluation.
Products that meet the requirements are authorized to bear the UL 3700 mark.
“By defining how these systems must be built, evaluated for safety and safely installed, UL 3700 helps mitigate potential risks, and opens a path for more people to access resilient solar power,” said Ken Boyce, vice president, principal engineering, industrial testing, inspection and certification, at UL Solutions.
While plug-in solar is simple to install and use, the potential risk is when systems become overloaded and power may flow back into lines. In addition to defining safety standards for manufacturers, UL says the new standard requires features that mitigate accidental contact with hazardous electric parts, promote safe installation, protect against overloads and prevent electric current from flowing in the wrong direction.
UL describes
in a white paper
the three main hazards of plug-in solar systems and how they differ from traditional PV technology.
Overcurrent protection challenges: Branch circuits are designed for one-way power flow from the panelboard to the load. When a plug-in solar system backfeeds power into the same circuit, the combined current from the utility and plug-in solar source can exceed conductor ratings without tripping the circuit breaker. This undetected overload poses risks of fire and electric shock.
Touch safety hazards: Grid-interactive inverters used in plug-in solar systems are not evaluated for user contact safety. Accessible plug blades can become energized when exposed to sunlight, creating a shock hazard for consumers.
Ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) compatibility: Plug-in solar systems can compromise GFCI protection, a critical safety feature in outdoor and wet locations. Current GFCI standards assume unidirectional current flow, but plug-in solar introduces bidirectional flow, potentially blinding GFCIs and leaving circuits unprotected.
The advantages of plug-in solar are ease of installation and cost. In terms of ease of use, “they’re literally plug and play,” Stephan Scherer said in a recent webinar. Scherer is founder of Craftstrom a manufacturer of plug-in solar devices.
As for cost, Scherer said the cheapest systems can be purchased today for under $500. “It’s way more affordable than traditional solar, currently at about half to a third the cost of traditional solar, he said. Currently at about $1.50 per watt, Bright Saver anticipates prices to fall precipitously in the coming year.
Payback time, like traditional solar, depends on the electric rate and how much the system is producing, but typically the payback period is between two and six years in the U.S., Scherer said.
As prices continue to drop in the coming year, several states are expected to pass legislation, further boosting the plug-in solar market. According to The
Q2 2026 edition of “The 50 States of Solar
”  released by the NC Clean Energy Technology Center, in addition to the ten states that have already passed legislation, Delaware adopted a resolution to study the safety and utility of portable solar devices, New Jersey and New York are awaiting final action by their governors and legislation is still under consideration in California, Massachusetts, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, and Pennsylvania.
